note: Accepts that risk-based regulation is the right frame but argues several provisions of the Act are not actually risk-based, and shows which levers exist to correct that during implementation.
title: Truly Risk-based Regulation of Artificial Intelligence: How to Implement the EU AI Act
explain_beginner: The European Union built its big new AI law, the AI Act, around the idea of 'risk-based regulation', meaning the strictness of the rules should scale up or down depending on how risky a given AI system actually is. This paper, a legal analysis rather than an experiment, argues that the AI Act does not actually follow that idea consistently. The author points out several mismatches, simple, predictable software gets treated the same as unpredictable AI systems in some cases, the categories of high-risk AI were decided in advance rather than case by case, and the law never actually weighs an AI system's benefits against its risks, it only looks at potential harm. The most powerful general-purpose AI models are singled out for extra rules based on a computing-power threshold that the author argues does not reliably predict real-world risk. Rather than proposing to rewrite the law, the author suggests the European Commission can fix many of these problems using guidance documents and legal tools it already has.
explain_business: Companies subject to the EU AI Act should expect near-term clarification to come through European Commission guidelines and delegated acts rather than a rewritten law, since the author argues today's high-risk categories were drawn too bluntly and are likely candidates for refinement. Firms building simple, predictable, rule-based software have a reasonable argument, based on this analysis, for why blanket high-risk treatment may not fit their product, since the author explicitly criticizes treating such systems the same as unpredictable AI. Providers of very large general-purpose AI models should expect continued scrutiny of the compute-based threshold used to flag systemic risk, since the author argues it does not reliably track real-world danger and may be adjusted. Because the AI Act overlaps with existing rules like the GDPR and sector-specific laws for medical devices and machinery, compliance teams should track upcoming harmonization guidance rather than treating AI Act compliance as a standalone exercise, since the author expects these overlaps to be a continuing source of duplicated or inconsistent obligations.
explain_practitioner: The paper is a doctrinal legal analysis measuring specific EU AI Act provisions against risk-regulation theory rather than an empirical study. Ebers's central critiques, pre-defined high-risk categories in Annex III create both over-regulation of low-risk systems that happen to fit the list and under-regulation of genuinely risky systems outside it, the general-purpose AI systemic-risk threshold is a computing-power figure that reflects political compromise more than a measure tied to actual risk, and the Act weighs only potential harms, never benefits, unlike a genuine risk-based framework. He also argues that applying a sliding-scale risk approach to fundamental rights protection is a poor fit, since rights violations follow more of an all-or-nothing logic, and that the Act's broad scope creates overlapping, sometimes inconsistent obligations with laws like the GDPR, the Medical Devices Regulation, and the Machinery Regulation. Rather than proposing new legislation, Ebers recommends the Commission use its existing guideline and delegated-act authority to refine categories and resolve overlaps. He acknowledges that risk-based regulation generally struggles to quantify unknown risks and cannot fully substitute for rights-based protection in every context.
